utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me start again. Today is Tuesday, the 17th of February, 2009. I would like to greet the accused, the counsel, the witness, Mr. Scott and his associates, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. Ms. Nozica, I would like to greet you as well, and I shall give you the floor, since you have three-quarters of an hour left.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I'd like to say good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar looked at me, because I forgot to give him the floor. He's got two IC numbers to give me. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. The OTP has submitted a corrected version of its list of documents tendered through Witness Buljan, Stipo. The now corrected version shall be substituted with the previous number IC 00924. And two parties have submitted their objections to the OTP list of documents tendered through Witness Buljan, Stipo. The document submitted by 2D shall be given Exhibit IC 925, and the objection submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit IC 926. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, once again. And once again, good morning to everybody in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, we can continue, can we not?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Where we left off?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, the transcript doesn't seem to be moving. I'd just like to correct something in yesterday's transcript. On 100, line 6, it said the witness said he was shown document 2D 2423, whereas the witness was shown 1D 2423. Mr. Vegar, at the end of yesterday's examination, we were discussing a document that -- for the transcript I'm going to give the number, P 3038, and that was the statement or announcement with respect to the event of the 30th of June, 1993, which was signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic and Jadranko Prlic, and was addressed to the information media. Now, you said that you had taken part in compiling this announcement, and I'd like to ask you -- ask you to take a look at 2D 00448, which is the next document in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Nozica. I may be wrong here, but I've just checked on my notes and there is a document in the transcript, 2D, and you say it must be 1D, but it is 01423. Was that -- did I mistake that or is it -- because now it says "21423."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my reference was that it was this document, but I'll check it out during the break once again and we'll see. Yesterday, I thought this was it, but I'll check it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, have you found the document?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I haven't got the binder.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness doesn't seem to have the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have checked it. You were right, it's "243." I was wrong. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It's the second binder, Mr. Vegar.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. You have the document. 2D 00448 is the number once again. Could you tell us, Mr. Vegar, at the outset, and we'll go into an examination of the document in due course, but could you tell us what this is about and whether you heard this speech yourself, personally?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This speech by Arif Pasalic, the commander of the 4th Corps of the BH Army, which he delivered on the 30th of June, 1993, of War Radio Mostar, is the day --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just please first tell me whether you have heard the speech. Can you remember that speech?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I heard it at 11.00, myself, but it was broadcast later on, and I think I heard it later on. And I heard it that day and the following day in transcript form.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: In paragraph 2 of this speech or announcement, it says: "Ustashas forces early this morning kept up their aggression against the BH Army and the citizens of Mostar by strong artillery fire and infantry attack on the positions of the 4th Corps units of the BH Army." Now, Mr. Vegar, I'd like to ask you to explain to the Honourable Trial Chamber what it is that happened on the 30th of June, 1993, and what information you personally had about what happened on that day.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early in the morning on that day, the forces of the 4th Corps attacked the barracks called Tihomir Misic in town, which is where the HVO forces were stationed, and also north of Mostar in the settlements of Bijelo Polje and along the defence lines towards -- facing the Serb forces. There were also attacks in the town itself at the separation line, so this is completely untruthful, what you just read out, that it was Ustasha forces. The Ustasha forces didn't exist. Now, the HVO forces did not continue the aggression. That was a total lie. And as I say, the attack came from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, you say that the attack came from the 4th Corps. Now, do you have any information to the effect that there was an attack by HVO members who were Muslims and who were in the -- within the HVO in the barracks that day? Did you have any information about that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the barracks itself, but also at the separation lines and in facilities where the army slept. Along that whole line, members of the HVO who were Muslims, ethnic Muslims, turned their weapons towards the people who had been their friends and colleagues up until that moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you have any meetings with anyone who had suffered any losses on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, one of our soldiers, well, his father and mother were killed in their home.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did you come across him that day?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Mr. Peric.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And where did his parents live?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bijelo Polje.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So we can note, then, that this particular sentence, the first sentence that reads: "Ustasha's forces early this morning kept up their aggression," et cetera, regardless of whether this is hate speech or propaganda, but the observation made that the BH Army -- by the BH Army that the HVO attacked is completely untrue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at this other -- this document and compare it to the statement signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic with the statement released on the same day with respect to propaganda and hate speech, and I'm going to focus on two other portions in this speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Pasalic's speech on the radio, what may seem strange is that he lays this at the door of Mr. Petkovic, Lazic, Vrlic and Tuta, but at no point in time does he talk about politicians. How can you explain this, because Pasalic is a military and he believes that this is a military matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A possible explanation could be this: The fact that Arif Pasalic was in the same Command with those people earlier on, that he spent time with them frequently, and even his free time, so I think he's addressing people who used to be his friends, but he's full of hatred in this speech.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to draw your attention to another sentence in that document, where he says: "The citizens of Mostar, Muslims and other honest citizens, beat the Ustashas at every step." That's in the middle of the text. And now the last paragraph -- or, rather, the last paragraph, yes, of this text, it says: "Citizens of Mostar, remember that this is a day of destiny, when you have to start your battle, and I call upon every able citizen who is able to carry a stone or a rifle to kill the Ustasha criminals, because there can be no life together with the Ustashas, except for life with honest Croats and loyal Serbs." Now, Mr. Vegar, may I have your comment to the fact that he refers to all Croats as Ustashas and calling upon the people to use stones to fight? So who, then, were the honest Croats and loyal Serbs that he refers to here?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, to clarify for the record, there's no statement -- it's incorrect for counsel to say that the document refers to all Croats and Ustashas as Ustashas. In fact, as counsel just indicated there's a distinction being made in this document, itself. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and I think I said -- thank you to my learned friend. I think I asked the witness to tell us who these honest Croats were and loyal Serbs, to whom this does not apply.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So I would just ask the witness to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Arif Pasalic here is giving himself the right to make judgements and decide who an honest Croat is and who a loyal Serb is. I think that that is completely unacceptable, because all Croats, all Muslims, and all Serbs are honest citizens until somebody individually proves the contrary. Now, I think that there are the vestiges of the communist ideology to be found here, because the Communists always used to say workers, peasants, and honest "intelligencia," and so a priori, they imply that there someone who is dishonest and only rare individuals can be considered honest. So Mr. Pasalic is doing the same, that there might be some honest Croat and Serb somewhere, but there were very few people who thought along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, Mr. Pasalic, is he calling on the citizens as well, not only combatants, because he says "citizens and anybody who can bare weapons and carry a stone," so he's calling upon the citizens and combatants and everybody to hit upon the Ustashas wherever they can?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's how this reads.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, let's just go back to the statement we were looking at earlier on signed by Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic on that same day. You helped compile that statement. You don't have to find it. I'm just going to say that it is --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: ... and whether there is any sentence there, any sentence at all, and I'm talking about document P 30 -- P 3038 is the document I'm referring to, whether there's any sentence at all to the effect that the side who was really attacked expressing intolerance, hatred, or incitement towards struggling -- fighting everybody on the opposite side?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't come across any hate speech in any sentence, or incitement to things like that in this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, thank you. Now let's take a look at another document, and we're still staying with the topic of your participation in compiling some press releases, or public announcements, or the like, and I'd like to ask you to look at P 02690 now. When you find it, tell me. As we see, this is an announcement for the 9th of June, 1993, the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, and I'm going to ask you now, Mr. Vegar, just briefly to tell us the circumstances under which things happened around the 9th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask that the microphones in the courtroom be switched off other than the one used by counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the time when the Muslim forces attacked the towns and settlements and HVO facilities in Central Bosnia. It was a dramatic state of affairs, and in this announcement mention is made of disagreement within the army commanders in the area, themselves, but also the political standpoints of the Muslim leadership, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I'm going to ask you to focus on the last paragraph of this document, where it says: "The head of the Defence Department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, addressed all the Croatian combatants and people with a message, telling them that our suffering must be put a stop to and that aggression must be met with an attack." And then he says: "Attached is the following:" Now, would you look at page 3 and see what was attached to this document. Mr. Vegar, did you take part in compiling this statement at all?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, explain to me, when you say that you took part in it, did you actually write it in agreement with Mr. Stojic, or did he say that this is something that had to be written and then you sat down and wrote it?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to the best of my recollections.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, in this announcement, does it say anywhere that aggression must be met with aggression or aggression must be responded to with aggression? And I'd like you to focus on the last sentence, where it says: "Anybody who shoots at you must be considered your enemy, and you have the right to respond in equal measure. We did not prepare for this war, but we have to accept it." Now, from this announcement, does it follow what was the free interpretation of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone, that Mr. Stojic said that aggression must be answered with aggression? That's my first question. Please answer.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic's address does not incite people to an attack, but what it talks about is the need to respond, that is to say, to people shooting at us, so it is a call to defend the people, to defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me now, if you can remember, why Mr. Stojic sent this letter. Can you remember what sort of information was coming from this area in that time, in June 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The news coming was about ethnic cleansing of Croats from that area, and also that commanders in that area, and units, were at the end of their tether. Some of them were even asking for a corridor to be opened so that the entire population could leave towards Herzegovina, to be evacuated.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: With this communication, is Mr. Stojic encouraging them to stay in their homes, or is he inviting them to come to Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is an appeal to them to try to defend themselves and stay where they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at 2D 5995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a follow-up question. You told us that you were the person who had prepared document P 3038. This document is signed by Mr. Prlic. When you prepared this document, did you turn to Mr. Prlic's inner circle and turn to these people and say that you were drafting this document in the form of a press release, or did you prepare this document, hand it over to Mr. Stojic for him to sign it, and then forward it to Mr. Prlic for him to sign it? Do you remember the chain of events or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I remember is that Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic were in touch and that it was their joint decision. That's how it reached me, this instruction that I should write it on behalf of the two of them. I think that's the way it went. There was no need for me to inform the people around Prlic. If he was aware of it, then it was his duty to inform his associates if he deemed it necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you please now -- you were talking about dramatic news coming from Central Bosnia just before the drafting of this communication and this news prompted you to write this statement. Can we now look at 2D 595? Did you find it?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is that one of the reports that emanated from Central Bosnia at the time?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can see the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we please -- can you please read paragraph 2 and tell us what it says?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: "We know that this is the last report we are signing. We, those who are politically and militarily the most responsible for the Croatian people of Central Bosnia, people who are forced to flee before the Muslim knife from their homes, even after more than 250 people were killed, slaughtered, numerous wounded and large numbers of disappeared civilians and soldiers."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about paragraph 3?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 3 speaks of the opening of the corridor, which is no longer a matter of days, but a matter of hours, and: " ... that is why we are asking for 40 soldiers to be sent from --" I can't read the name of the settlement, "... to secure the corridor and shelter the suffering population, and we are forced to break through towards you anyhow."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. So this letter -- this situation, I'm sorry, this situation depicted in this communication prompted that statement by Mr. Stojic. I would now like to move to a new subject. I don't know how much time we have left, but I'd like to look at 2D 41 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. I have a follow-up question. This document, which I believe stems from Colonel Tihomir Blaskic, Mr. Kostroman, Valenta, and Colonel Dario Kordic is addressed to Mate Boban and to the chief of the Main Staff in Mostar. I don't see that the minister of defence is one of the recipients of this document. Is there an explanation for this, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only logical explanation I see is Mr. Boban had asked Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic to react. They came to see me, and that's how this response came about.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, we're talking about the document dated 8th June. Don't confuse these two things. The document 2D 595, please tell the Court again how you came by your information.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought the Judge asked me why Mr. Stojic reacted when this document was sent to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that was not my question, sir. I'm sorry if this was not conveyed to you properly. This document, which stems primarily from Colonel Blaskic, but who seemingly -- which seemingly was signed by the people -- we don't have the signatures. We have the feeling that it was sent in the form of a telegram or a fax. So this document was sent to Mr. Boban and to the chief of the Main Staff, but the minister of defence is not mentioned. And when you look at the document, you see that the situation is disastrous, so much so that Blaskic, in the fourth paragraph, say that they are currently destroying all documents. One can visualise this very well, and he finishes off by saying goodbye, so we have the feeling that that is the end. In a scenario of this kind, how is it that the minister of defence is not one of the recipients of this document? This is my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why those under-signed, those four men from Central Bosnia, did it this way. I can only guess they sent this to Mr. Boban because they thought him the most responsible for the situation they were in, and they thought him the most able to help them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. Second question: This document stems from the Command of the Operational Zone, so it's a military document, and you can see that it says "Confidential, military secret." So this, normally speaking, is a military document. How is it that civilians, in inverted commas, like Kostroman and Valenta, signed this document? What does this mean? Do you have an explanation to give us or don't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my explanation is this: The situation was so dramatic, so catastrophic, that they felt the need to write and sign a document jointly to make an even stronger impression to the recipient to drive home how serious the situation was and to elicit a response in the form of some action.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, what makes you say that Mr. Kostroman and Mr. Valenta signed this document? I do not see any signature on the paper that is in the file that I have received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this paper -- we've already mentioned how difficult it was to send communications from Central Bosnia. This was sent by packet communications, and that does not allow for personal signature, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Still, the question then arises whether Mr. Kostroman and Valenta are not other addressees, whether this does not mean the document has also been copied to these two gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that is not possible, because in the very body of the text it says: "This is the last report we are signing, we who are the most responsible politically and militarily."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this package transmission, does that account for the fact that in the B/C/S document it is stated "8th of June, 1993, 1613," so it must have been received at 1613?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the operators of these devices would mark the time when they received the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours, but because of what Judge Trechsel asked, I'd like to go into whether Ignac Kostroman, Anto Valenta, and Dario Kordic are perhaps recipients.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Could you go back to paragraph 2: "We know that this is the last report we are signing, we who are the most responsible, politically and militarily, for the Croatian people of the Operation Zone Central Bosnia." Tell us, were Mr. Kostroman, Anto Valenta, Dario Kordic and Tihomir Blaskic indeed the most responsible, politically and militarily?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, Mr. Anto Valenta was the vice-president of the HVO HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What about Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Him, too. He was vice-president of the political party HZ-HB.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now have 2D 00418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry. I still have questions regarding this document. Witness, do you have any idea as to where it was set up and signed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I could not know where it was drafted, but I believe that it was drafted at the military command of the operation zone, because they were the only ones who had the technical capacity to send such communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And does it seem plausible to you that both or all three, Kostroman, Valenta, and Kordic, were also there? One gets the feeling, reading this, that it is written in the field somewhere, with shelling all around, and the idea that, "We have to retreat, flee, or we will all be killed." Now, that these four high-ranking people are all at the same time in that place, in that zone of high danger, does not seem very plausible to me, but maybe you can explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, you're right. That area where the HV [as interpreted] was in Central Bosnia was so narrow that there was physically no location that was out of reach for shells or shooting. Whether the four of them were exactly at the same place at the same time, I don't know, but I know that this document was sent with the consent of all the four of them because they were very aware of how serious the situation was. And it was not just a moment; it was a situation that had lasted at least for months by that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: This then, nevertheless, leads to some doubt whether they actually -- you said "signed by" when I asked you how do you know that it was signed, and assuming, which I would think natural, that Valenta and Kostroman were somewhere else, in Grude, Mostar, whatever, and had perhaps by telephone or radio given their consent, joined this appeal. Is that a possibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, theoretically, that too is possible. Why not? I have to repeat, I don't know where they were physically at that moment, but this document did arrive, and as far as I know none of the four had ever denied authorship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At line 21, page 16, something has to be corrected. It was "HVO," not "HV."

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: For the third time, could you please look at 2D 00418. Have you found it? You have to skip two or three documents, because we don't have enough time. Now, would you be so kind as to explain this? You spoke about the education of fighting men. You said that you were participating in the work of the IPD sector, educating fighters about conducting armed conflict. This is a brochure. Did you distribute such brochures? How often did you have these education drives? Was it -- did they look like this?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So on one side, the rules of conduct for fighting men, and on the other side, first aid. This is the document we see in front of us, but in fact this is what it looks like. Could you now tell us, what was this education like, who participated, how often, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We organised meetings with workers of the IPD and commanders of units to familiarise them with the rules of conduct in war, treatment of civilians, the wounded, et cetera, and we had the help of the International Red Cross, and we got these documents from the representatives of the International Red Cross in Croatia because this document is in the Croatian language.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, when you had these meetings with the assistant commanders for IPD, did you supply these booklets for them to hand out to the fighters, and did you give them instructions that at the level of their units, they should provide information to the soldiers about how they should behave?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did hand out a number of brochures of this kind, and it was their task to inform all the soldiers with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now I'm going to show you another document, and I'm going to ask you to comment on it and tell us whether you know about it. It is P 4626.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in this booklet. I'm looking at the photograph in the B/C/S document, because in the English version there is no translation of the photo. We can see a house on fire in this photo, and there is soldiers, and there is a woman carrying a child in her arms. Next to her, you can't see whether this is a man or a woman, and then an old man stooped on his cane, holding something in his hand. And the soldier in the foreground sort of waves to him and tells him to go somewhere. Well, this rank-and-file on the ground, the soldier who had this booklet and saw this situation with a woman and an old man, what is that soldier supposed to do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The soldier must assist. It is his duty to assist civilians, wounded persons. He must be humane in his conduct. He must not loot their property, must not mistreat them, and so on. He must take care of these civilians, take them out of the combat area, if they are in jeopardy, until the fighting stops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please proceed, Ms. Nozica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now let's look at P 4626. I'm sure you've found it.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me what this is about? We've seen this document in the courtroom before, and there seems to be an unsavoury joke at the end. Could you tell us who compiled this document? Have you seen it before? Can you explain it? It says: "Published by the IPD, the HVO, the Operative Zone South-East Herzegovina." It's called "Aktuelnosti." Did you know that such a -- there was such a publication? Have you ever seen any copies, and have you seen this particular issue?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know that the IPD published a document, the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina. As we see this is number 59. Of course, I wasn't able to read each and every issue or take part in compiling it. Now, as far as this last paragraph is concerned, which is titled "Auschwitz," I think that it is an impermissibly bad joke which can be interpreted as an expression of national hatred, ethnic hatred, although we know that our culture is one of jokes, a joke culture, usually not very appropriate jokes, and there are quite a lot of examples of telling jokes at one's own expense. But of course in a bulletin of this kind, there is no place for a joke like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: You said, "I was not able to read each and every issue of the bulletin or take part in its creation." Did you take part at all in creating the bulletin for this South-East Herzegovina zone?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Who, then, was the author of these bulletins?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The IPD of this particular operative zone.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Although it is very unpleasant, we have to explain what you meant when you said "inappropriate," "istasan" [phoen] or inappropriate jokes, and this rude sense of humour which is present, but there are also jokes at one's own expense; right? Now, as there's implication here and refers to Suljo and Muljo, who are obviously in Sarajevo, just to first to understand, are Suljo and Muljo personages that appear in jokes all the time, like Rudi and Bobi [phoen], or Joe Blow or Joe Smith, whatever, and -- or are they specific characters?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not specific characters. They are characters the names of which are used in most jokes. And when there was the energy crisis with gas from Russia, for example, in Sarajevo, jokes were going 'round on a similar topic about Auschwitz and gas supply.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar said that it was inappropriate and should not be found in a publication of this kind, especially during a war. Am I right when I say that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to ask us to look at another document, 2D 4 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm now turning to the paragraph on the Croats in Muslim prisons. It is stated here -- and this document dates back to August 1993, so it states that in Mostar, allegedly, there were 110 soldiers and 450 civilians detained. Where were they detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So back in August 1993, in East Mostar there were 110 HVO soldiers who were prisoners and 450 civilians who were detained; is that how we should understand the situation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't say exactly whether there were 110 or 450, I didn't write those figures, but I think that I can believe them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us speak about Zenica. There were allegedly 1.500 civilians there. Is that plausible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is plausible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I forgot one thing. This is information coming from Mr. Pusic? That's what's stated in the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Probably the editors of this bulletin took that information over from Mr. Pusic, because they say that that was a quote from him.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I know how much more time I have left?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vegar, we're going to move on to another area that I would like to address, the distribution of pensions to all the citizens of Mostar in 1993. First of all, let me ask you whether you had a pensioner in your family who, at the end of 1993, received a pension, and did you know that pensions were being handed out at the end of 1993 to all citizens?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have information about that. They weren't pensions according to what was due the pensioners, the pension earned. It was a linealary [as interpreted] remuneration according to the funds of the HVO at the time. And my father-in-law was a pensioner, and he received this sum of 50 Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you have 17 minutes left, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to look at document 2D 818 now, please. It is information to me, my name, and I'd just like you to confirm to the Trial Chamber that the Federal Institute for Pensions and Invalid Insurance is, in fact, an institution which is the sole institution authorised to provide information about pensions and the like. Am I right, Mr. Vegar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And this is a document dated the 20th of July, 2007, signed by the director, Nadir Kovacevic. Now, in this letter he refers to a meeting and agreement that my team had with him, but what is important here and that I'd like to highlight is the following: It says in paragraph 1: "With regard to the implementation of the pension and disability insurance in 1994, we hereby inform you that on the territory of today's Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were two insurance companies, the Social Pension and Disability Insurance Fund of BH, with its headquarters in Sarajevo, and the Pension Insurance Fund of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, with its seat in Mostar." And then in paragraph 2, it talks about the application of the Decree Law on the Adoption of the Law on Basic Rights of Pension and Disability Insurance passed by the Government of the HR-HB as a basis for paying out pensions, and in paragraph 3 it says that right up until the 1st of January, 2002, when the Federal Pension Institute was established, that these two social funds paid out pensions. It says: "... and all the citizens of Mostar who earned their pension on the basis of the Social Pension Disability Insurance Fund or who were to be granted entitlement to pension disability insurance, exercise their entitlement through one of the insurance companies. The remit of an insurance company at the time was in accordance with actual situation in the field." Now, Mr. Vegar, from this letter, from the Pension Insurance account fund from BH, the BH federation, we see that all citizens who found themselves in the area of Mostar had the right to receive pensions, that is to say, on territory that came under either the Social Pension Fund from Sarajevo, with its seat in Mostar, or the Social Pension Fund of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. And you said that you had information according to which the assistance or -- pensions or remuneration was handed out to all citizens in 1994?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. This document accurately reflects the situation as it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right. Now let's look at 2D 821, which is the next document, and it is a decree to which this letter refers passed on the 20th of January, 1994, regulating the right to a pension entitlement. Now look at document 2D 826, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. While he's doing that, I just wonder if we're back to reading documents again. What's the basis of this witness, a public relations officer, talking about decrees on pensions? And all we've done so far is show the documents in front of the witness and ask -- counsel asks if she's read them correctly, so I wonder how much the witness can assist us with any personal knowledge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that the next document is going to continue the demonstration, D 826.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, might I be just allowed to answer my colleague. With the document, I wanted to show the source of these documents that I'm presenting now, because as we can see from the document, 2D 818 [as interpreted], it says that these were payments that can be seen in the archives of the pension fund. Now, as this witness says he knows about pensions and how they were paid out, I am showing him these lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you found the document, 2D 826?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, but maybe counsel can assist us, then, by explaining what the basis for this witness to talk about pensions. She's just -- she's made the assertion that he knows, but I haven't heard any evidence from the witness about how he's involved in pension matters and can address these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, could you ask the witness what his personal knowledge is of this issue of pensions?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness said himself, his father-in-law was a pensioner at the time, and he knows that the HR-HB compiled lists, kept lists, that's his knowledge. And he knows specifically a person who received a pension, and that was his father-in-law received a pension on this basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. My grandfather used to receive social security benefits in the United States. That was my grandfather, but that doesn't make me an expert on social security.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Mr. Scott's grandfather was a very lucky man, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have a few minutes left. Please finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would have completed my examination, had I not been interrupted, and the witness can tell us what he knows and then the Prosecutor will be able to cross-examine him on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you looked at document 2D 826?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, here it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Tell me, this is a list of pensioners who received assistance in money for the Christmas holidays and new year holidays, and it refers to one specific local commune. Which one is it? Can you tell us which local commune?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bijeli Brijeg 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Does that settlement exist in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: And now we have a list, 1 to 24 on page 1.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, in our proofing session we looked at the names. Now, did we conclude that there were at least 11 Bosniak first and last names of persons who received pensions? For purposes of illustration, look at this list.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was common knowledge that everybody who had an entitlement to a pension received a pension, and I think that we established that on the basis of the previous document that we received from the present Federal Institute for Pensions. The Social Pension Fund confirmed that everybody who had an entitlement to a pension received one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Well, we'll go through other documents. 2D 827 is next, and tell us when you have found the document.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: What local commune is that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Centar 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Did something like that exist in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Have you looked at the list? And I'd just like to draw your attention to the fact that we have 52 names on this list, and we looked at the list together and found that at least 29 Muslim names or Bosniak names are on the list; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, look at the next document, which is 2D 828. Would you please tell me, this is Local Commune --

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Cernica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Cernica. Is it also in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, there were some local communes in Mostar. Was it the case that in Mostar even before the war, there were larger concentrations of Muslims or Croats in some local communes and more or less evenly distributed population in others?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can you tell us, area by area, where there was a majority Bosniak population, where there was a majority Croat or a mixed?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim Bosniak population was mostly on the left bank of the Neretva, but there were numbers of them on the right bank. Some outskirts of Mostar had a majority population of Bosniaks before the war, whereas outskirts on the west were almost exclusively Croat. You can see that from the census of beneficiaries of pensions by local commune.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can all extra microphones be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is local commune Strijelcevina? "Strijelcevina," correct. Obviously, if you look at the first page, we can see that there is a list of names, and all of them are Bosniak names. Is this one of the local communes where -- with a majority Bosniak population?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: 2D 830 will be the next document. This is Local Commune Zgoni. Did such a local commune exist in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: One of the rubrics is the amount and the signature of the beneficiary. Now, please, look at document 2D 824. This is a list of beneficiaries of pensions, with forms for payment for 1994, through the Hrvatska Bank?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, Pension Insurance Institute of HR-HB?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Look at the number 1119. It's Pero Grubesic. Was that your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, from all these documents, we see that the Croatian Republic Herceg-Bosna at that time in end 1993 and on in 1994 was distributing pensions to all beneficiaries of pensions, regardless of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Is this consistent with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Can we now look at P 5984.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have that document.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: It should be provided separately in the binder.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps at the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: We provided it later. P 5984. You can look at it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: This is the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, 20th October 1993, a table depicting pension beneficiaries, broken down by local commune. It's signed by President Ante Cvitanovic. Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Here we see local communes located in Mostar and some around Mostar, such as Potoci, Rondo, Ilici. This data here, is it consistent with the number of beneficiaries who received aid and pensions in the beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It looks pretty realistic to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, we see at the bottom that by ethnicity, by ethnic composition --

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that document somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: -- there were 5.246 Croats, 2.107 Muslim pensioners, 698 Serbs, and 90 others, according to this list, made on the 20th October 1993. And my final question, having looked at these documents: These pensions were distributed to all beneficiaries of pensions under the control of the HVO; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, according to the actual situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: So, yes, that's what I wanted to ask you. All the citizens under the control of the HVO received their pensions?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: That would be all. Thank you very much for your answers. Your Honours, I've completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm going to object to this. And I know because of the lapse of translation, perhaps we already have the answer, but this is -- I've objected before, and I don't know why the Chamber doesn't exercise more control over the propriety of the evidence that it's receiving. This witness cannot possibly confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't allow you to criticise the Judges, "I'm surprised that the Chamber does not control." Control what? Defence counsel is currently demonstrating, on the basis of joint criminal enterprise in Mostar and in Herceg-Bosna, 2.000-odd Muslims received a pension. What do you want us to control?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... confirm that. He has no personal -- he talked, he surveyed each of the recipients, and they received their benefits cheque in the mail? This witness cannot possibly testify to these facts. He cannot, he cannot. This is pure speculation on his part. Now, if he wants to say, "I've talked to -- I surveyed, I telephoned them all on the phone and they confirmed to me that they each received their cheque in the mail properly," et cetera, et cetera, that might be evidence. This is sheer speculation. The evidence can -- the witness cannot possibly address this. That's why I objected at the very beginning, some minutes ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Vegar, some time ago, on a question of Defence counsel regarding these different villages, your answer was, page 29, line 23: "It looks pretty realistic to me." You recall that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember. It looks rather realistic to me, compared to the ethnic composition of the population then, and the proportion between pension beneficiaries of one, second, and the third ethnic community looks pretty realistic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And when you say that you know or you affirm that everyone got their pensions, is that also more or less saying that it is realistic or something like that, or do you actually know that each and every one got his pension, as you have affirmed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was a commonly-known fact that everybody received pensions, regardless of ethnicity. And I think that it's completely wrong to expect me to know whether each and every person signed the receipt, that they received it or not, but it's a commonly-known fact, confirmed several years later by the most responsible people, directors of the institutes for pension insurance, such as Mr. Kovacevic, and I believe it's a credible source, it's a fact we can believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as far as the knowledge you had is concerned, from what I understood, your stepfather received a pension; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note, father-in-law probably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you talk to your father-in-law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the course of your conversations, did he say that he and other people received a pension; he may have also told you that Muslim neighbours, like him, also received a pension, or did you never discuss this matter with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I talked to him, and he expressed his surprise, saying from what sources -- from what funds HVO was able to distribute pensions, because nobody else distributed pensions in Bosnia-Herzegovina, meaning the population in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina under the control of the authorities of the ABiH or Republika Srpska. It may be a coincidence, but my wife worked at the bank and she also paid out these pensions, after they started to be paid out through the banks several months later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So your wife was working in a bank and said that she paid the pensions out. Did she say that she paid these pensions out to the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please, I would like to respond to the objection of Mr. Scott very briefly. In the Prosecution case, we did not see any evidence to prove that every name or every incident happened in the way the Prosecution claimed. They provided, instead, documents containing endless names, and it was up to the Court to judge the value of such evidence. This witness commented on the official documents of the official authorities that governed at this time, and he spoke of his own experience relevant to the documents. I believe both are relevant. He confirmed, first of all, which official authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina were able to provide this data, and how they provided it, and he said what he knows personally about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may with only two words to add to what my colleague said, my learned friend from the Prosecution objected, saying, "What makes this witness qualified to speak on this subject or other subjects?" Let us just remind ourselves that during the Prosecution case, we have seen a large number -- not just a few, a large number of foreigners, journalists, members of the ECMM, members of the UNPROFOR. Some of them spent in Bosnia all of two or three days, and we heard their testimony over several days, their observations, and all sorts of problems, that I have to say, most of them had no clue what they're talking about, and we clearing up this gradually and slowly through our case. Some of them, even the majority of them, were certainly not qualified to speak on the majority of subjects they actually did speak about. We did not object. It was up to the Prosecution to call whoever they wanted. We had another example - now the colleagues remind me - of a lady, a witness who was illiterate, and she interpreted here before this Court a military document and its significance. So those were the criteria that applied. We can't change them now. We can't have the Prosecutor change them, the same Prosecutor who insisted on those criteria. And we remember his explanations when he said that those were the circumstances that prevailed, We cannot provide better evidence, et cetera. We can't change the criteria in midstream, or we can if we go back to the beginning of the trial and start over again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall now have a 20-minute break and resume after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel has an hour and a half for its cross-examination. Mr. Ibrisimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have no questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Prlic Defence, we have no questions for the gentleman, but we do wish to thank him for coming here to give his evidence, and we yield our time to the Praljak Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as Praljak's -- right. Praljak Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness. The Defence of General Praljak, in its cross-examination, will refer to the direct examination or, rather, examination-in-chief of the witness, recorded on page 20, 21, line 21 -- 25, 21, lines 1, 2 and 20; page 24, line 7; page 61, lines 17 to 21; page 70, line 19; page 72, line 12 to 19; line [as interpreted] 69, lines 11 to 15 of the transcript of the 16th of February, 2009. The relevance of the questions in the cross-examination of General Praljak is to be found in the paragraphs of the indictment, and they are: 15, 17(d), 17(l), 17.3(k) and (m), paragraph 27, 31, 33, 39(b), paragraph 100, 101, 112, 116, 133, and paragraph 238. So those, then, are the references in the indictment which provide the Defence team the right to raise the questions and go to their relevance with respect to the observations made by this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Vegar.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Ms. Alaburic, are you going to take the floor after that or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, we will have questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And how much time have you allocated, Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that all the Defence teams will be able to get through their cross-examinations within the hour and a half allotted to us. And as I'd like to address the questions raised by the Trial Chamber, and if I need a few extra minutes, I will ask the Trial Chamber's indulgence for an additional two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And Mr. Coric's Defence counsel?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... reached a final decision in the matter, but we will state our views in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I think that we will be able to conduct the cross-examination within the time allotted to Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, I'd like to correct certain matters from the transcript that were recorded yesterday so that we don't have any wrong information and wrong testimony. Mr. Bozo Rajic, whom you succeeded, became minister of defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'm asking you that because in the transcript, on page 20, line 25, and page 21, it says that Bozo Rajic became minister of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you worked in the paper "Slobodna Dalmacija," it's a newspaper which is published in Croatia; right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But you did not work in Croatia; you were the editor of "Slobodna Dalmacija" in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a correspondent for "Slobodna Dalmacija" in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: You didn't work in Croatia at that time?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And that was recorded on page 21, line 20. Thank you. Let's move on. During the examination-in-chief, at one point, and this was recorded on page 20, line 16, said -- you said that the war broke out, there was a war during that time, and you also said that you were first a soldier and then an officer. And that was recorded on page 24, line 17. I'm now going to ask you the following: What war were you referring to, and where were you a soldier, and where were you in 1992, up until September 1992?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout the time until my involvement in the Defence Department, I was a journalist and correspondent from Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. So that means you lived in Mostar and you can provide information about what you saw, heard, or experienced in Mostar personally or learnt directly from somebody close to you?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Right, thank you. May the witness -- ah, you have the documents in front of you. Right. From the first smaller set of documents, would you take a look at the following documents: 3D 03267 -- and I'm going to read out the numbers of the documents, and then I'll ask you one question relating to that set of documents. 3D 03268, that's the next document in order. 3D 03269, 3D 03270, 3D 03271, 3271, 3271, 3D 03271 -- yes, that's right, that's the right number now, and three 3D 03272. These documents are approvals with your signature on them, and in them you approve journalists and television crews and journalist crews to go to Heliodrom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And is that what you were talking about during examination-in-chief when you were talking to Ms. Nozica about enabling foreign journalists to acquaint themselves with the situation in the area of HZ-HB?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to open document 3D 00785, and on e-court it goes with 3D 00785-1. Mr. Vegar, are you familiar with the book "Urbicide 1992"?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you come to know about it at greater length so that we can lay the grounds for asking you questions about it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, before we address "Urbicide," what I'm interested in is the permission you gave journalists to visit the Heliodrom. When you gave this permission, were you the only person to decide to allow international reporters to go and visit the Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can confirm that, as far as the permission goes, I was the one who permitted the journalists to go, in agreement with Mr. Bozic, the warden of the prison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The co-director, therefore, agreed to let international media visit the Heliodrom to see what was happening in that detention facility. Did you, yourself, know what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did have some information about it from the journalists, and they emerged from the questions -- that emerged from the question they asked, because they had information from other sources. Sometimes they proved to be correct; sometimes they proved to be incorrect. And I had information that I heard informally, rumours going 'round town, and I said that I went with a Red Cross team twice and a team of journalists to the Heliodrom military investigatory prison. Now, what I know, therefore, is on the basis of those visits and what I heard from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know, Witness, we have had witnesses here who were in the Heliodrom, and they told us what the detention facilities or conditions were, and you said that you had been to the Heliodrom. When you went to the Heliodrom, were you able to talk to the people who were in the detention facility there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, for a very brief period of time with two men who were held there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you talked to two people who were detained there. And these two people, did they tell you why they were being detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I asked them what the conditions were like and whether they had any complaints and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You, yourself, didn't know why they were being detained, or did you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't know. All right. You don't have the names of these two people you talked to; you don't remember, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, unfortunately not. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to your recollection, were these people civilians or military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These people were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- military men.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let's go back to my previous question, which was: Can you tell us, in greater detail, how you came to be acquainted with the book "Urbicide 1992"?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that a book of that kind was being prepared. I know when the book was promoted, and I know that -- or, rather, I'm sure that there was some photographs in that book which I took.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Which you took personally?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took them in the second half of June, I believe, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the transcript. Would you now look at 3D 36/1156 or "-1156." In English, it is 3D 36, page 36-1172, and 1156 is the Croatian. We have a subtitle where it says "Bridges." The next page, Mr. Vegar --

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I take a moment. What did you say, "Mostar"?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. The subtitle is "Bridges," and that subtitle says that it -- that Borislav Puljic wrote this. Do you know the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Who is he?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a well-known Mostar architect.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Have you read the text before the pictures of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Can you confirm, to the best of your recollections and knowledge, that the bridges were destroyed, the first bridge in the night of the 24th of May, 1992, and that was the Lucki mosque?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the other microphones kindly be switched off in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the answer which was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Could you repeat it? Do you know that the Lucki Bridge was destroyed on the 24th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I seem to remember that that was the case. I don't know the dates off by heart. I know that Lucki was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, can you confirm that in the period up until April, May and June, Tito's Bridge, Carinski Bridge, the railway bridge in Rastani, that they were all destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the bridges were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to look at page -- it's 13 in the book itself. On e-court it is 3D 36, that's the number of the book, "-1158" is the page number. The subtitle is "Housing." And for Their Honours, it is page 3 D 36-1174 and 1175. Mr. Vegar, Almas Bavcic [phoen], Jasmina Cehijic [phoen] and Meviha Perzic [phoen], do those names ring a bell? Do you know those individuals?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know them personally, but I've heard of them. I know who they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know what their ethnicity was or is?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they declared themselves as Muslims at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know who worked on this book? Was it only Croats or did the Muslims or, rather, Bosniaks take part in its -- in writing it?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: They worked together.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, in this section entitled "Housing" or "Collective Housing," would you look at the penultimate paragraph, where it says that: "In this war --" And what war is that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the war at the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: With whom or against whom?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the Serb Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It says: "In this war, everything was destroyed, even that which never served war purposes. Whole settlements of the old urban structure of the town, the Mahala, Carina, Luka, Donja Mahala, Karadjol Bego Mahala [phoen], Fajic [phoen] Street; on the left bank of the Neretva, the settlements of Podhum, Zahum, Balinovac -- Podhum, Zahum, Balinovac, Fernica [phoen], were brutally destroyed and seriously destroyed. Also, new urban structures for individual housing, the residential districts of Cim, Jasenica, Zalik, Bijelo Polje, Buna, and Hodbina have suffered equally heavy destruction and damage." Now, Mr. Vegar, Podhum, Zahum, Balinovac, Zelenica are they all parts of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Which parts of the Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the central part of Mostar on the West Bank of the Neretva.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, were these neighbourhoods damaged and is this true?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, look at the paragraph just below "Collective Housing." The authors are Zoran Bosnjak, Nerica Eminovic, and Maida Ljubovic. Do you know these people or do you know them by reputation?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: By reputation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: From this passage, I'd like to ask you to look at 3D 36-1159, which is the next page, the passage about intensity of damage to collective housing. Where in Mostar were apartment buildings, not individual houses?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the eastern and the western part. In the western part, there were more of them. You mean apartment buildings built after the Second World War for collective housing?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us -- can you identify which parts of Mostar? For instance, Cekrk, did it have apartment buildings, that is, for more than one family?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was it was -- there was a hotel there, I believe Soko, or, rather, a low-rent hotel, and also apartment buildings for workers who worked there.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about Rodoc, Centar 1 and Centar 2; did they have apartment buildings?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Centar 1 and 2, I believe most of the buildings are apartment buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: These areas, Centar 1 and Centar 2, are on the west bank of the Neretva; right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Rodoc is in the southern part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During examination-in-chief, the issue of destruction was not dealt with, so the time you are taking to speak about that is going to be taken out of the overall time you were given, because this is an altogether new topic you're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak agrees. We believe it's an important topic, too important to have it skipped, but we agree that it will be against our time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I just wanted to ask you about Rodoc. It's a neighbourhood at the exit from Mostar, when you go south?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And in that area, there were also apartment buildings, and they were also damaged; right? Now please open to page 3D 007 -- sorry, 36-1160. Mr. Vegar, please, we did not get a record, your answer, when I asked you about Rodoc. There were apartment buildings there, and they were damaged? And your answer was?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Right. Now please look at 3D 36-1160. The subheading is "Infrastructure Systems"; author, Zoran Bosnjak. From this text it follows, and I'll ask you if this is consistent with your knowledge, that with the destruction of the bridges -- infrastructures ceased to exist because the main infrastructural facilities went by these bridges?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because pipelines, telecommunication cables, electrical cables all went via the bridges.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that in 1992, the transformer station Cule was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I believe for two or three months a good part of Herzegovina did not have any power for that reason.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What about long-distance transmission lines and network?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was also damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Please wait a second after I finish my question. Otherwise, we won't have the questions or answers on the record. In this text, it says that among the first to be hit was the PTT communication building, so that around 35.000 telephone subscribers remained without telephone. To the best of your recollection, and in view of the job you were doing at the time, did you know about the damage to the PTT building in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was damaged, but the people who worked in the PTT building, according to my information, had expected that the PTT building might be targeted, so that one exchange remained undamaged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have an important question that can encapsulate the situation. Based on this text, I want to know this: Whether you can answer my question or not, I don't know. As to the situation in Mostar, before there was a conflict between Muslims and Croats, was the situation there the result of the Serb attacks that had destroyed bridges, that had shelled the water supply system, the power network? Was the situation the result of the Serb actions or was it the result of a conflict between Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mostar was devastated during the Serb aggression against Mostar in the beginning of 1992. You can see that from this book, but also from many film records. All the bridges were destroyed in 1992. The infrastructure, such as the electrical supply network, PTT installations, water supply, all met the same fate.
