I believe it would be an overstatement to say that the conflict between Muslims and Croats arose only because of that. It was partly a result of the previous conflict, and all the consequences that followed from the Serb aggression against Mostar and that part of Herzegovina; primarily the large number of refugees flowing in from Eastern Herzegovina into Mostar, the change of the demographic picture of Mostar. But Mostar cannot be viewed in isolation from all the other events in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. I can see in this text I have in front of me that the generator of the Cule station of 400 kilowatts was totally destroyed. The one in Rodoc, 110 kilowatts was also destroyed. Apparently in Rastani and in Opine, the same was done. So was all this destruction done by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the destruction occurred in Mostar or in surrounding places, did you see that there was no more decent power being supplied?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that also true for the water supply yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you experienced that personally, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you remind us of where you lived at the time, for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lived in a part of town called "Panjevina." It is still called "Panjevina."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I guess it is in West Mostar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, the residents in West Mostar, did they feel the consequences of all the destruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Yes, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, I'd like to ask you just, in order to save some time, just to look at the photographs of the mosques destroyed, and this is particularly important to me because of paragraph 116 of the indictment, which says that the mosques were destroyed in 1993. Please look at the Hadzi Mehmed Bey Karadjoz Mosque, page 3D 361235.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Then 3D 36-1237, the Nesuh Aga Vucjakovic Mosque?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And then picture 20, 3D 36-1239, Koski Mehmed Pasa Mosque, and page 3D 36-1245, Dervis Pasa Bajezidagic?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And page 3D 36-1246, Tabacica Hadzi-Kurta Mosque, and another mosque on 3D 36-1247. Mr. Vegar, these pictures were taken in 1992 [Realtime transcript read in error "19"]?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: At that time, these mosques were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now please open document 3D 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat the number. 3D 03101. I'll ask the witness to answer one of the previous questions again because it's not on the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I asked you about the mosques that I enumerated. At that time, they were destroyed or, rather, damaged?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And your answer was?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Your Honours, and I apologise to my learned friend. It would be too complicated. At page 49, line 3, my colleague asked: "Were these pictures taken in 1992?" And the year was not recorded properly. It can't stay that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you know Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: This part of the cross-examination refers to yesterday's direct examination and the questions by Judge Antonetti on Ahmici and the relationship between Muslims and Croats, that is, the Army of BH and HVO, so I would like to ask that this not be deducted from General Praljak's time. You know Mr. Ismet -- Dr. Ismet Hadziosmanovic personally?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadziosmanovic is by ethnicity is a?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Why should this time be not taken out of your time?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the current questions that are about to follow, yes, I believe they should not be deducted because they were raised yesterday in direct examination. The evidence was about Trusina, and you asked the witness about Ahmici. That's why I think it should not go against our time.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: If we look at this -- I'm a bit thrown off, but I'll try to get back on track. So you know Mr. Hadziosmanovic, you know he's a Bosniak, and you know he wrote this book, and you, like him, were there in April 1993, in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to look at this part of the text, the first text, where it says: "On the 16th of April, 1993, in the morning hours, HVO units committed a crime against the Muslim civilians in the village of Ahmici."

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In the morning hours; right? And I apologise. The page is 3D 35-1092. For the Court, the page is 3D 40-0037 and on. The next passage speaks of the attack of an equestrian brigade of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina committed in Trusina near Konjic in the early-morning hours of the same day?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And that's what you spoke about yesterday, the things that you know about, these attacks that happened. And then he says, "Both armies committed war crimes on the same day." That's what Dr. Hadziosmanovic says?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: At the same time, on the political level, intensive talks were going on between the Municipal Board of the SDA and the Municipal Board of the HDZ. Is it your recollection that these two municipal boards of the SDA and the HDZ met to try to resolve this situation and calm things down?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know about this passage in the book, where it says that members of the BH Army, that is, the Mostar Battalion, and members of the HVO came out into the street and marched together to show their protest and to try to prevent the conflict between Muslims and Croats? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember any of that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I see, you don't remember it well. And you cannot remember that -- well, Dr. Hadziosmanovic writes here that understanding the very dramatic situation, very serious for a possible border conflict, the HVO and the BH Army, the Regional Board for Herzegovina issued two public announcements, and after that the armies went out together which wished to show their dissatisfaction and endeavoured to prevent a possible war in Mostar between the HVO and BH Army. So I'm going to ask you this: Your recollections, do you remember that efforts were made to avoid a conflict in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Now, in 2000, and we heard this during the examination-in-chief, you were in the office or, rather, the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina; right? You were employed there?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: While you were working in the Presidency, you had information about the laws that were passed; is that right too?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you happen to know that a law on the return of property was passed?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know that according to that law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, please. Witness, counsel is now moving on to another topic, but I'd like to remain with Trusina and Ahmici. You said that you knew the author of this book. Page 185 of his book, second paragraph, he mentions Ahmici and Trusina. These two locations are not mentioned in our indictment, but from memory I believe that Ahmici was mentioned in the Prosecution's pre-trial brief. A professional judge, such as I, in such a situation, before thinking of tu quoque, has the following question: Were the attacks in Trusina and Ahmici related to one another, and should there be a link between the two attacks, which was the first, which was the second? This text gives no answer to the question, because it was it was that -- it was the morning that the HVO attacked Ahmici and also during that morning the ABiH attacked Trusina. You, yourself, maybe you can't answer this, and then the question we'll put to other witnesses, if need be, but from what you think in terms of time, what was the first attack; was it Ahmici or was it Trusina, if you know? If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollections, the attack in Trusina was the first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you believe that the attack in Trusina was the first. How far are the two towns from one another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the crow flies, I think about 80 to 100 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eighty to one hundred kilometres, I see. All right, thank you. I won't have any more questions for the time being. Of course, I can ask the question of military who will be called to testify. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: A follow-up question to that. Mr. Vegar, do you know, before the 16th of April, 1993, in the area of Konjic municipality, whether any conflicts took place and whether there were any clashes between the HVO and BH Army before the 16th of April, 1993, if you know about it?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do know that before the attack on Croatian villages around Konjic, around the village of Busa [as interpreted] and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Buscak is the village. I'm saying this for the record, Buscak. I asked you a question related to your knowledge of law and law enforcement, and you said you knew that a law on the return of property was passed. Now, what I'd like to ask you about that is this: Upon the cessation of the conflict between the BH Army and the HVO, do you happen to know anything about whether people exchanged apartments, whether people from the West bank crossed to the east bank -- the Muslims crossed to the east bank, for example, and did they -- did people exchange flats, did people migrate within Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, flats were exchanged flat for flat, but very often people sold their flats on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That's right. Now, if we were to analyse the flat situation, would you agree with the conclusion that I'm going to put to you, and it is this: That during 1993, at least 4.000 Muslims, and possibly up to 7.000 Muslims, were on the west bank of Mostar in the area under HVO control?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, several thousand Muslims throughout the war lived on the west bank under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'll wind up my questions, and then General Praljak will be asking you questions linked to his participation in the events contained in the indictment, of course if the Trial Chamber permits him to. Now, Mr. Vegar, doing your job in the Defence Ministry, did General Praljak ever order you, ask you, request, or suggest that you issue statements, whether public or otherwise, that is to say, public announcements to all citizens or internal announcements for the members of the HV [as interpreted] brigades, battalions, companies or whatever, asking you to write incorrect data or give false information so that with the soldiers and Croatian citizens, you incited hatred of the Muslims and fear of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can state that quite resolutely. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Line 55 -- or, rather, page 55, line 9, it is not the HV but should be the HVO. I wasn't talking about the Croatian Army, nor do I intend to at the present.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vegar, did any of the six accused here in court ever suggest, order, request, demand, or whatever, that you publish information, either internal information for soldiers, brigades, areas of responsibility, or public announcements in which you would incite hatred in any way towards the Muslims and cause unfounded fear of the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, Mr. Vegar, in the public announcements, or press releases, or whatever, did you ever consciously and intentionally write things that were incorrect; did you fabricate events to put into these statements or announcements?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never consciously. I never put down any fact that I consciously knew to be false.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: When you reviewed the reports of the IPD in the brigades and areas of responsibility that came in to you, did you ever establish in any one of those reports something was consciously or intentionally written that was false and untruthful?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollections, no, no, that any -- I never saw anything that might have been consciously or intentionally fabricated.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Vegar. Now, with the Court's permission, General Praljak would like to take up the questioning at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, the Trial Chamber reminds you that you are allowed to ask questions in -- due to your competence or because you were, yourself, involved or concerned by a specific document. I'm saying that in order to avoid any issues of objections.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will adhere to your instructions, that is to say, that I ever had personal knowledge, or took part, or it's a military question. Cross-examination by Accused Praljak:

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Vegar.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Look at 3D 03266, please. That's the document I'd like you to look at. Did you know that I, in 1992 and 1993, up until the summer or thereabouts, I was the assistant minister -- assistant to Minister Gojko Susak in the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia for information and psychological activity?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right. This document deals with the 12th of October -- 3D 03266 is the document number that I repeat.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that in the bigger binder or the smaller binder?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: It's the smaller binder, 3D 03266, and it deals with a visit by a team -- a group from the department that I headed, and pursuant to an agreement reached by my head, Dr. Anto Mijatovic, a visit to Herceg-Bosna. And at the seminar that took place, a lot of people had been invited to attend, some 40 guests. Now, do you know that this cooperation existed at all and will to help from the Ministry of Defence and the department that I headed vis-a-vis you?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know that the International Red Cross and the booklets and brochures that arrived down there arrived with assistance from the department that I headed?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let's take a look at this document now, which speaks of many things. I don't have time to go through everything that it addresses, but general tasks are mentioned. There are headings such as "Information," the assessment of combat readiness, and things like that, and what happens and what the consequences are of the poor flow of information. Then it talks about victims. Do you know that all those were enormous problems that faced an organisation like that, a fledgling organisation?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Towards the end there, it talks about HVO units and the differences between making political decisions, implementing political decisions, that is to say, the role and place of the army. And then the relationship between the democratic authorities and the army, that's another heading, and the difference between state, political, and party politics, and the observations made is that there is no place for party politics in units. Were all these subjects that you had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and we tried to adhere as much as possible to these basic principles; that is to say, that the army can only be - how shall I put it - a service. It cannot make political decisions itself, and also that party politics has no place in military units, although sometimes we did have pressure in certain municipalities from some officials, party officials, when it came to employing, say, a certain cadres, but we did our best to resist pressures of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And now finally let's see what the problems were that occurred in the army. And it said the lack of response to mobilisation and the lack of implementing corresponding sanctions, and the over-burdening of fighters at the front, and then the multiplication of political problems in certain areas inhabited by Muslims; Mostar, Vakuf, Bugojno. And then it says that it is expected that through coordinated action, the government, which at the level of a conflict -- had risen to the level of a conflict, will be resolved, because the problems can have unforeseeable consequences on the military plane. And then it goes on to talk about the non-systematic resolution of problems for invalids, wounded, and fatalities. Now, from all this, Mr. Vegar, does it follow that in fact there was a terrible programme -- a terrible problem in the army, such as the wounded, the killed and so on and families, and because of our financial situation, could not be solved across the board, but was solved from one municipality to the other?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers kindly slow down and speak one at a time and avoid overlapping. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Next, an important thing in this Tribunal -- I do apologise. Go on, Vegar, answer.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Objectively speaking, it was very difficult to help the families of those who were killed or wounded because of the lack of financial funds, and some municipalities were richer than others and they then attempted to solve the problem, whereas others didn't, especially municipalities which - how shall I put it? - were on the battle-field, that is to say, that were along the front-lines and the separation lines. They suffered more and weren't in a position to deal with the problems facing them.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Vegar, the problem of mobilisation, in other words, that one could not control mobilisation, that people didn't have to respond to the mobilisation call-up, they could go to Croatia?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the border was opened up, and I think I said yesterday, by quoting an example of military psychologists, et cetera, that 70 to 80 per cent of people from the area escaped to the Republic of Croatia and that they weren't able to be mobilised, although they were very necessary, and that's what happened with many others, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And what was to be done, faced with a situation like that, and the establishment of power and authority, that the authorities couldn't do anything about the mobilisation call-up? What did you hear from the army and the soldiers? They said, "We don't receive a salary, some have fled, so what can you do to us if we decide to go home"?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a great deal of frustration among those up at the front-line. They were quite simply angry at those who had left, who had fled, and they asked that mobilisation be implemented. They also asked that sanctions be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And the other thing, Mr. Vegar: A soldier who was ready to lay down his life and stay to fight, was it very important for him that if he were to be wounded, that he would be taken care of, and if he were killed, that his family would be taken care of?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And, finally, I have here the last line of that page, it says that Croat crime was on the rise and what to do about it, and the question of sanctions, especially the lack of clarity about the armies and the civilian authorities' responsibilities. So what can you tell the Court, at a time when a country is dissolving, disintegrating, and all its structures disappearing with it, what ability do you have to conduct investigations, to implement sanctions, and to take to task perpetrators of crimes through legal procedure?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time, the possibilities for doing that was minimal. You couldn't undertake legal action, the proper kind of legal action, because as we know, the judiciary and the court system was in trouble, just like all the other systems.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That completes my examination or, rather, this part of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have a follow-up question for you. This meeting which was held in October, did you attend this meeting or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't there myself, but people from my section were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did you not attend this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because somebody had to stay behind, somebody had to stay on duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If you'd been there, I would have had a whole series of questions to put to you. But since you weren't there, I won't put these questions to you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, please look at 3D 03228. It's a newspaper called "The Herzegovina Soldiers," published by the 4th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and what I'm showing you is an issue of February 1993. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know about this paper?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I held it in my hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Open page 1, 1st January 1993. Let's just look through so that the Honourable Judges can see what all the writing was about at the time. It says Chetniks have shelled the first lines of defence in the urban area on more than one occasion. It's about Konjic, and that shelling died down after the joint response by Suad Alic Brigade and Stjepan Brigade, Herceg Stjepan Brigades. There was some destruction. Do you see that? Do you see that? It's for the 1st of January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I'll ask you the question at the end. Let's just go quickly through the text. Then 8th of January, members of the independent company Blagaj from the composition of the 1st Mostar Brigade took the solemn oath. The text of the oath was read by the youngest combatant, Amer Tanovic, and the commander, Midhat Hajdor, expressed his gratitude. You knew them?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: "Congratulations, followed by Djafer Effendi Sahic and Safet Memic on behalf of the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as well as from Zrinko Puljic, the commander of the 8th Battalion of the HVO." Is it clear from this that at that time, the 8th of January, the cooperation between the HVO and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was at such a level that the oath-taking ceremony of the ABiH was attended by representatives of the HVO, and they offered their congratulations?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Look at the 9th of January. Again, the Chetniks opened artillery fire on Konjic and the positions of the 7th Cavalry, and they used also anti-aircraft machines guns and the response was fear. 27th of January. After a long break, the Chetniks are shelling all parts of Mostar; twenty civilians wounded, one unfortunately killed. And the 23rd of January, the same thing, 16 people wounded. 24th of January, shells falling on Mostar, Stolac, Konjic. 25th of January, shelling is dying down. The Chetnik offensive is crushed. 26th and 27th January, it says: "The offensive is crushed, the Serb Army's offensive is crushed, but as a rule, after a defeat of the Chetniks, a retribution follows. The highest-calibre shells are targeting towns and cities. Civilians are being killed." 30th January: "Responding to a fierce attack, the fighting men of the 3rd Battalion of the HVO and the 1st Battalion of Bregava destroyed one Chetnik bunker and two tank shelters, tank bunkers." The 1st of February, an attack on Stolac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Praljak. I don't quite see where the question is and where you are going. Is it again the matter where you read a long document and then you ask the witness whether he agrees, or do you expect the witness to be able to confirm every piece of information that you are reading out, or what? Could you please explain to the Chamber what the purpose of this is, because we are a bit lost, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the purpose is very simple, I believe. My question is going to be, and I can ask it already now: When you live in a town and when the enemy forces are targeting you every day with 100, 150, 200 shells, and your women and children and soldiers are dying, then the issue of primary importance to this trial is what is going on in Mostar, what is the mindset, how hatred is rising, how in that situation is it possible to defend several hundred Serbs who stayed there? The question is: Did the Serbs shell Mostar continuously? That's one question. And the second question: Does the cooperation between HVO and ABiH continue throughout, in combat, in oath-taking, in everything? Those are the key issues about which somebody living in Mostar at the time had first-hand knowledge. And when you look at Mostar at any time of night or day, without any military justification, the town is shelled all the time, it remains engrained in your memory, and that's what my question is going to be. And since this is a newspaper published by the 4th Corps of Bosnia-Herzegovina Army, we shouldn't doubt its credibility, because if I were giving these facts myself, then you could interpret it differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: So I also would like to say, Mr. Praljak, that again that the hatred and the vengeance, it is not the issue which we are talking about here, and it is what I also already mentioned yesterday. I had already mentioned yesterday that in this case it will be an endless discussion about what happened in Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1992 to 1995, et cetera, and we would never reach an end of it. The question is: What are the actual situation here, as far as in the background of your questions? Do they affect in any way or are they in any connection with the indictment? Or what is the purpose of your question, as was also asked by Judge Trechsel? And again, I say that the issue of vengeance, the issue of the hatred, is not what we are dealing with here, and really I would like to ask you to take this into account in your questions and whatever you are asking. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, this is a delicate issue because there can be varying points of view and diverging points of view on the Bench. As you said, this is an unquestionable document from the 4th Corps, and the position of the enemy which is expressed in this document. I don't wish to discuss the issue of hate speech. I only focus on facts and what do I see in this document. And this comes to me as a surprise, because I had not understood that the Serbs were involved at this time, and so involved at this time. If this document speaks the truth, we can see that throughout the month of January 1993, the Serbs were shelling Mostar, the Mostar area. And according to this document, there is a joint action of the HVO and ABiH against the Serbs. I feel, therefore, that this document is highly important. One thing, Mr. Praljak, and this is where I agree with my colleagues. You must put your question in a clear manner. As Judge Prandler has said, you must not put the words in the witness's mouth. He does not need to confirm this. However, you should put your question in such a way that one can reach a conclusion, so that the Judges are informed about the situation. This is what we are asking you to do. You discussed the 1st of January, the 8th and 9th, the 20th of January, so put your question now to the witness. If you don't know which question to put to the witness, I do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I know, too, how to ask him questions, but how will I do it if you don't allow me to use documents that you, yourself, say are important?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: So, Witness, to the best of your recollection, in all that we saw written in this newspaper, what is not true?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that anything is not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge from living in Mostar, are these reports correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports are objective. Whether there were 50 or 60 shells is another matter, but that shelling was continuous and daily, not only in this month. If the Court allows me, I can confirm that the shelling from Serb positions did not stop, not even in 1994. And I know very well that the last shells fell on Mostar on the 3rd of August, 1995. I know that because one of them broke the windows in my apartment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in Mostar in January, well, you were living in West Mostar. That is something we know. Did you have the feeling that at the time the conflict was between the Serbs and the HVO and the ABiH or was the conflict between the Croats and the Muslims, the Serbs were holding their position and cast a neutral eye on all of this and woke up from time to time and shelled from time to time just to manifest their presence? You were a player there at the time. How did you perceive the situation in January and February of this year? That said, this document, at first hand, bears the hallmarks of a reliable document, indicates that in Stolac at the time there were Serb attacks also, and the HVO together with the ABiH counter-attacked the Serb offensive. This is my question: As a resident of Western Mostar, did you have any information about the fact that the conflict in January was a conflict between the Serbs and the HVO or the ABiH or was it a conflict between the HV [as interpreted], the ABiH, and the Serbs mere onlookers? I would like to ask the court reporter not to type "HV" but "HVO," please. So answer, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My understanding then, as that of most people in Mostar, Croats and Muslims alike, that it was a war between Serbs on one side and Muslims and Croats on the other side, and not only in January, but in the months that followed as well. I will remind you of what I've already said; that on the 30th of June, Muslims and Croats in the HVO were on lines north of Mostar, facing Serb troops north of Mostar, as well as in Velez to the south-east of Mostar. And concerning that conflict between Serbs and Croats, I and other people used a milder name. We did not call it "war," even when it escalated in May and June in Mostar, because we always thought that the negotiations that were underway between officers of both armies and the politicians of both ethnic communities at peace conferences will bring a reconciliation and an end to the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I would like to correct something on page 67, line 25. It says that "June," and the witness referred to the 30th of June many times, but which year? It would be useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 30th of June of what year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood correctly, on the 30th of June, 1993, alongside each other, the ABiH and the HVO were facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were together in the same trenches facing Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were in the same trenches; in other words, alongside each other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the same positions, and that's when this betrayal occurred, and the men who had been together in the same army, wearing the same uniform, with the support of the same logistics and weapons for more than a year, turned their weapons against one another. On one side, there were members of the Muslim ethnic community who disarmed their fellow fighters, and the BH Army [as interpreted] took control of the entire area, or almost the entire area north of Mostar and the Tihomir Misic barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, in other words, you have added that the ABiH had disarmed members of the HVO, which means that they were able to take the northern barracks in Mostar, so I bear this in mind. Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, may I be allowed to say something, Your Honours, and to make a slight correction? Not members of the BH Army, but members of the HVO who were Muslims. Muslims within the HVO, they unleashed this process that you mentioned, and with the BH Army's help, they disarmed many, arrested others. There were a lot of dead that day. And then the attack north of Mostar started as well as south of Mostar and west of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an important clarification. The Muslim soldiers of the HVO disarmed the Croatian soldiers of the HVO, with the help of the ABiH. This is what you're telling us. But how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what I said. Well, I know about that, I know about the composition of those units because I, myself, toured those lines north of Mostar on Mount Prenj where there was a military HVO unit, and 70 per cent of it was made up of Muslims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, on the 2nd of February, just to complete that, it says that a Chetnik offensive occurred on the Stolac battle-front and that the attacks were refuted. And now look at the next page, sir, where it says: "Fighting and not Politics." That's the title, and it says there one of the goals of this paper was to raise morale and combat readiness for the 4th Corps. And then it goes on to say that many didn't ask themselves -- failed to ask themselves why they were fighting, what they were fighting for. And the answer given is: "At all events, the basic goals of the fight against the Chetniks, from the beginning of the Greater Serbia aggression against our young fledgling republic, remain unchanged. A free and sovereign Bosnia and Herzegovina within the nationally-recognised borders, open to coexistence and whose internal setup will mean that everybody who considers these regions to be their homeland will be able to reach an agreement on." Have you found that text?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vegar, was that the main stand of all HVO structures in Herceg-Bosna and did they remain constant?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the HVO and, in this particular case, the BH Army too.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Yes. Now, this article, does it differ largely in matters dealing with a unitary Bosnia-Herzegovina or, rather, a united Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, turn to the next page and let's look at what it says here about Pocitelj and the Pocitelj Ravens or Gavoranorji [phoen], and then the first column, where it says: "The war began here on the 6th or 7th of April, when the Chetniks launched a breakthrough across Mount Bivolje," and then the action to transfer Croats and Muslims across the Dubrava elevation and the Neretva River. And we already know that 12.000 or 15.000 people were transported in a short space of time. Now, do you know about this event, that all the Muslims who had, first of all, stayed on at the Dubrava Plateau were transferred across the Neretva River together with their cars and everything else?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we're between answer and question, I assume for some minutes now, once again we've been on Mr. Praljak's direct examination time, since this has nothing to do with cross-examination. I assume this is time from their case in chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber will see whether some time should be deducted from your time in relation to this question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, it says here combat groups in the tunnel and the right bank are being organised, and then in brackets it says it's interesting to mention that the first lilies were brought here by the then defence commander Cetin Luburic [phoen], and that says something about the relationship of the Muslims and the Croats of these regions and their mutual respect. And judging by everything, it is -- this unity is inviolable. Now, do you know who Mr. Luburic was?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time he was under my command there?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Is it correctly stated here that the first lilies -- and lilies are the emblems of the BH Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Anyway, that the first lilies were brought by Mr. Luburic to the Muslim fighters, that is to say, Mr. Luburic, being a commander -- former command of Capljina defence?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, we have one other matter here. It says at the time, in an APC which was seized, Sasa Zurovac was caught in Mostar as a criminal of Ahmet Hadzic and so on, and they set up the first flag with the lily emblem on the left bank of the Neretva River. Now, does it say here that in crossing the Neretva River on the 16th of June, 1992, the Muslim combatants had raised a flag with their own national symbol on the department store, at the top of it?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And then it goes on to say: "After the liberation, Dubravko Kapin, that group, were victorious and returned to Pocetelj, where Alika Petanovic [phoen] put up the first flags with lilies on the tower of the mosque, and this occurred on Bajram." From this, is it clear, sir, that the Croats, well, not only didn't they mind any Muslim emblems, but they helped by bringing in the lily emblem as co-combatants in the fight against the aggressors; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now take a look at the "Armageddon over Bosnia." That's on page 2 -- or page 7, and he says here -- well, have you heard of Sefkija Dziho?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, many times, Sefkija Dziho.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Let me read this out. He said that the service was made up of basic security elements, and then he says in Konjic, for example, in recent months we had nine cases of killings. We had five killings in the military police in action. Now, do you know that regardless the fact I keep debating this point with His Honour Judge Prandler, whether during the war the number of killings, to the best of your knowledge, for reasons that we're going to clarify, did they increase, and the possibility of detection of the perpetrators decreased?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Right. Now, let's look at the next page, the 6th Fleet from the Neretva River. That article is written by Camil Sahovic, and that's the last article; and it says with the arrival of the service in the Dubrava region, we began preparing for an armed struggle together with our neighbours, the Croats, led by the late Pero Dalmatin. Do you know about that, do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know about Pero Dalmatin.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, the next column towards the end goes on to say the following: "After that, there was a short period of reorganisation in the HVO so that the battalion was disbanded, and we then had this present unit of ours. And in that unit, we have solely Muslims, and we're the best unit in the brigade, which they recognise in the HVO, and we've become popularly known as the 6th Fleet." From this, sir, can we see whether the Croats had anything against, after the liberation of Stolac and Dubrava Plateau, the Muslims formed their own Muslim detachment?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, we can see that, that that was the case -- or, rather, not the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And then later on it goes on to say: "Through our efforts, we gained great respect within the HVO, and the BH Army knows about us, too. They know our worth and just how many of us there are." And then lower down it says: "All my soldiers bear lilies and have been doing so from the very beginning. And as far as that is concerned, the HVO makes no problems for us, because ultimately we're all fighters of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then at the end, it says: "These combatants can serve as an example to their own people and the Muslim people, although they gain their affirmation within the HVO ." Now, Witness, in these articles written by Muslims in February 1993, were there any indications at all of any kind of mens rea or thought that the HVO would in any way like to subjugate -- expel and subjugate the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can see that they have full trust in the HVO, and nothing of the aforementioned, and that they are completely along the line or follow the course of a joint struggle, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, as to this issue of emblems or insignia worn by soldiers, we had an HVO soldier testifying, and here it seems to be a document coming from the Muslim side, in which it is said that Muslim soldiers in HVO units would have the insignia of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know what this refers to, to which time. Mr. Praljak says it was written in February 1993. He may be right. I don't know. But as far as you know, did you know that there were Muslims who were members of the HVO and would bear the insignia of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, I knew that, and I saw it. Some of them carried only lilies, and others on their sleeve would have the lily and the HVO coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just said that you saw it. Where did you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, I saw them in the units, and I was in the 1st Brigade, for example, which was part of the BH Army there. I saw it on the streets, on the battle-front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, let's move on. Well, since we're on this subject, let me ask you about the 12th of June, 1993 [as interpreted], two days before the crossing of the Neretva River with the HVO action and some units of the army that existed over there. In Sutina and Uborak, 114 Croats and Muslims were killed, of which -- or, rather, who killed them?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb units.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: That was in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, north of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: I have to make a correction. It wasn't 1993, it's 1992, so what I meant was the 12th of June, 1992. Since, on a phenomenological level, the Prosecutor wishes to extract a theory about a joint criminal enterprise, now, you're a journalist, how can an event like that where 114 people are killed, some of them thrown on a rubbish heap, how can an event of that nature reverberate in town among their friends, relatives, brothers, and so on, in that destroyed town that it was? What happened?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was general bitterness because of this event, in fact. There was fear. Some tried to flee straight away because they thought that the same fate might befall them. And at that time we have to know that the Serb Army had complete control of the east bank of the Neretva River. And I know that the people whom you mentioned, some of them were taken from shelters and cellars, because most of those people took refuge in shelters and cellars because there was shelling on a large scale. Thousands of shells fell on the town, so people took refuge in cellars and basements in the surrounding areas and apartment blocks, and you had people of all ethnicities. They were all together, nobody separated them. And unfortunately, if I can put it that way, I was a witness of the suffering of those victims, and I think that I filmed the scenes of when the remains of those victims were dug up in Uborak.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now, in Mostar, in South Camp, you had the Yugoslav People's Army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: At North Camp, you had the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: At Ortijes, at the airport, was the air base?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And Heliodrom was a military base?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: In the Soko industry and factory, producing parts for aeroplanes, you also had JNA officers controlling manufacture?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they produced airplane parts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And that was all in 1992. Now, during the attack, can we agree that a large number of officers of the Yugoslav People's Army lived in flats throughout Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: And before the aggression and the beginning of the aggression by the JNA on Mostar, did they flee Mostar?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they pulled out of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Now I'm going to refer to Exhibit 3D 01027 [as interpreted], which are books, in fact, admitted into evidence, and the witness has said that they are authentic. And I'm going to ask you, Witness, to take a look at this large binder that I had mentioned, 1206, 3D 1206. Now, you didn't compile the tables. That was done by my team, under my control and instructions, and I will be responsible for that part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There must be a mistake in the transcript. It must be 3D 1026.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, 3D 0106 [as interpreted]. I just referred to 3D 01027 as being a collection of books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a problem with figures, Mr. Praljak. I think it's 3D 1026.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, I really do have a problem with numbers. The number is correct, and it is the document that I'm showing, 01026, 3D 01026, but I was referring to Exhibit 3D 01027, which were books on the basis of which a database was compiled, a computer database, and on that database we have calculated tables and graphs which I would like to show to this witness here and now. It's all been translated for Your Honours, and this is a super precise -- or, rather, a super precise analysis would take a lot of time, but the matter in hand is quite a simple one, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. Could we have a little information about where all this comes from? Most of it is not translated. It's pages and pages of material, apparently. Can we just have a bit more information so the courtroom can appreciate, or not, what this is?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. This was the question I'd asked myself. Do explain where the document comes from, who drafted it, in what year.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, of course I can. The witness, who had books, these books, authentic books, established there was book 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, as a foundation, as a database, and that number was accepted as 3D 01027. And based on that, a database is developed the way it's done with computers. You have to put in binary code numbers, that is, 0s and 1s, so that the relatively unsophisticated device, which is the computer, could make tables.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, but who wrote these books 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6?

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prlic Defence brought here Mr. Borislav Puljic as a witness. Through Mr. Puljic, we introduced at the time those five books made by Urbing, and there is a page attached here that says that they were made by listing apartments in 1992. Mr. Puljic verified that those were indeed these books and that based on the books we can draw reliable conclusions for purposes of analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Go ahead, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, still -- I'm sorry. I still have to ask, now that we have this bundle before us: What is the idea of having pages and pages, 254, with columns where one has a number 1 at different places? I'm not a computer, I cannot read this, nor are other members of the Bench. I fail entirely, entirely, to see any value in this, and I would like to have an explanation. I must say I find slightly offended by being confronted with this. It looks a bit like when my computer wants to print out a picture in letters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Trechsel, what a scientific analysis of apartments abandoned by Serbs over a couple of months can provide you with, other than every number -- the number of every tenant, made in such a way that a judge, or the judge's assistant, or the assistant of the judge's assistant, can check. Anyone who wants to deal with the problem whether the HVO and the HDZ acted consistently with the joint criminal enterprise or, alternatively, that it did its best under the circumstances, and I mean really the best in regard to the apartments, most of which were allocated to Muslims, not Croats, what else can we do than put it before you? If I made this documentation myself, you would say that I am a liar and a frivolous man. You have, this way, the opportunity to check, and the Prosecution can check it too. All this is available on a CD-ROM. As well, if you want to check, you see on page 1 what kind of a database it is and how the data was derived. The original foundation for the database were the five books that were confirmed here as reliable sources of all this information. I don't know if you really have all the time to deal with this, but we are all attending the longest trial in the history of international justice and I'm taking it very seriously. So when I put something like this before you, I hereby express my respect. I don't want to offend you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's save time. If I understand properly, when a witness -- Defence Witness Puljic was called by the Prlic Defence, five books were submitted to the Trial Chamber. Based on these five books, you are attempting to demonstrate that contrary to the Prosecution case, when it came to distributing apartments, there was no discrimination and that apartments were given to people from all ethnic groups or all ethnicities. And if you look at the pie chart to be found in the document, you can see that there were 27 per cent for the Serbs, 35 per cent for Croats, 38 per cent for Muslims. Is that what you are trying to demonstrate? Because if you are trying to do that, you can put one question to the witness in one sentence, saying there is a thorough study that was carried out based on charts, very extensive charts, as to the number of tenants, and it appears that the -- and we have the following distribution in percentage. You can ask him whether he agrees or not, and that's gaining time for everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Antonetti, thank you very much. That is precisely what I wanted. The witness has had a look at this, but I believe it's clear, when somebody's doing very serious work in appreciation of the Trial Chamber, it is their duty to present something like this. I hope you will appreciate the enormous work that stands behind this, and that includes the opportunity to verify all this of the.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Witness, you've had a look. Is it in fact the case that according to the data, we favoured the Muslims and they got more apartments abandoned by Serbs than the Croats, in view of the proportionate -- proportions of the population?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, but it was logical, because there were more Muslims who were left without homes, who crossed over to the west bank, where there were more housing opportunities, because the apartments that belonged to the former JNA military personnel were mostly on the west bank.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: Another two brief questions. First of all, when a soldier is killed in Mostar, when there is shelling, everything -- it's a big -- it's big news, and when a child is news, it's even bigger news. Everybody knows about that. And, third, in a state of war, when pensions are distributed, is there also a news item?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: What kind of news would it be when -- if Croats got their pensions and Muslims didn't? Would it be of planetary importance?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: But if 2.000 Muslim pensioners received their pensions, from all we know about that time, there were 7.000 Muslims and 1.000 Serbs, approximately, living under the control of the HVO in that part of town throughout the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED PRALJAK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions. And Your Honour Judge Prandler, I completely understand what you are seeking, but the Prosecution is trying to develop a theory that out of some phenomenological level, he wants to develop a theory about the joint criminal enterprise, and we don't know what the idea was, and the idea has to do both with thoughts and emotions, et cetera, because in estimating what could be done about something like that, what the possibility of control was. I cannot defend myself successfully if some sort of evil is ascribed to a perfectly organised system, a machinery that does not punish that evil just because it doesn't want to punish it, not because it's simply impotent, because it's deprived of any normal well-organised structure that every modern state has, and even such well-organised modern states sometimes have difficulty punishing crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, for everybody to understand this issue about flats properly, can you confirm -- I don't know whether this escaped some people, perhaps. When the Serbs left Mostar, the flats which were then available were occupied by Muslims and Croats? Can you confirm this, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was so, with the proviso there were more Muslims because they needed housing more at that time, they were more needy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying that there were many more Muslims than Croats benefitted from these flats. We moved on fairly quickly. This has to be put in the right context. You said that the Serb officers of the JNA were in West Mostar, which means that Muslims occupied flats in West Mostar? Can you confirm this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Most of the JNA apartments were in the west part of town. The military personnel left in the first days of fighting or even a few days before, because they knew very well what they were planning, and the east part of town was completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You yourself lived in West Mostar. The 9th of May, 1993, as far as I'm concerned, is a key date, and that is a starting point. Now, from this date onwards, were you made aware of the flats that Muslims in West Mostar resided in these flats since Serb JNA officers had left those flats, were these Muslims asked to leave these flats? This is a crucial issue. That's what I would like to elicit from you. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there were individual cases when apartments were taken improperly, in general, but I don't know of a single case when an official institution ordered that such flats be vacated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us an example? I don't know the street name, nor the number, but when you lived in West Mostar during this period, were you aware of the fact that there were -- you had any Muslim neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, I did have Muslim neighbours. There were not many Muslims living in the neighbourhood where I lived, because it's a new neighbourhood. I know that some of them continued to live there throughout the war. I know that some had left town as the fighting intensified. They went deeper into Herzegovina and into Croatian Dalmacija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you anticipated my question, but my question is an important one. I would like it to be recorded on the transcript. Now, among those Muslim neighbours you had, did some of them stay in the flats they were living in for the entire period of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you give us a name, for instance, someone you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't recall now, but there are thousands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We still need to hear the Petkovic Defence. We'll have the break. The Coric Defence perhaps also. Judge Prandler has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I know that we have to have the break, but I would like to make a few comments, in view of the fact that Mr. Praljak personally addressed me, and of course I would like to answer to him very briefly, to the point, I hope, and of course knowing that I may not convince him. But, anyway, I will do my best. Number 1, nobody denies your right, Mr. Praljak, that within the very established context and confines, you have the right to present your own questions when it is really important and when they are relevant to the given issues. Number 2, yesterday I twice quoted that rule of the International Customary Law and International Customary Humanitarian Law, which is, in shorthand, called "tu quoque," that there should not be any reciprocity established as far as the implementation of those rules of the International Humanitarian Law, IHL in brief, should ask us to follow. Number 3, you mentioned the question of the joint criminal enterprise. Of course, here we are to discuss this matter, and we are pleased to receive any information and any evidence which are proper, and to study the issue further. On the other hand, frankly, I do not think that the joint criminal enterprise can be explained by atrocities committed by any side of the conflict, and again I would of course have to add at least the commission of those crimes, but, anyway, we are dealing with those issues, and frankly again I do not see the link established between atrocities and the issue, in general, of the joint criminal enterprise. And, finally, that is why I am really -- I really felt, when I spoke, then you asked the questions, that those questions were about the morale, about the hatred, about how the soldiers reacted to this or that events, atrocities which were committed here and there, in Trusina, et cetera, and again I say that these issues of morale and hatred and other issues cannot be the leading motives as far as your behaviour or the behaviour of those forces which were there which would explain everything. And, therefore, I am still of the conviction that we should avoid those issues which are not related strictly to the issues contained in the indictment. That is my position. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's have the break now, because the tapes are running out. I shall take the floor when we resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, this is a continuation of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon Mr. Vegar and everybody else in the courtroom. I should first of all like to tell you the contents of my cross-examination, Your Honours, and please listen to me too, Mr. Vegar, so you will know what the topics I will be addressing are. The first topic relates to Arif Pasalic's speech over the War Radio BH on the 30th of June, 1993. My questions will be directly linked to the questions asked by His Honour Judge Antonetti as to why Arif Pasalic makes mention of the military commanders and not the politicians. And if I think that I have enough time, I would like to indicate -- to show some documents to Their Honours that show that Tihomir Blaskic, the commander of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia, as a rule, informed the head of the Defence Department, because I don't wish, on the basis of just one document, it appears that one commander ignored the head of the Defence Department. The third topic would be the report of 1993 or, rather, statement -- or, rather, the article appearing in "Slobodna Dalmacija" under your name, Mr. Vegar, and I'd like us to see what the foreign press said about this, how you present -- you were presented in the foreign media, and the Prosecution on that basis concluded that you were the spokesman for the Main Staff, and that statement was in fact a statement from the HVO Main Staff. Now, the fourth topic relates to the horizontal and vertical organisation of the Sector for Moral Guidance, and for the most part you spoke about that, but I'd just like us to hear extra explanations of your views on the basis of documents that you're familiar with. The next topic relates to the source of information, and you, Mr. Vegar, quoted a series of information sources on the basis of which you were able to comply with your job of informing the public and providing internal information, but also the -- it related to the report from the Main Staff or, rather -- and I would like to present a more balanced view and then explain the topic. And then a topic that goes beyond the frameworks of the examination-in-chief and relates to the collegium of the Defence Department, the way in which the senior staff meetings worked and whether the collegium was a collective body or not. Now, if Their Honours agree with my assessment that that is, indeed, outside the scope of the examination-in-chief, I will agree that I spend just three minutes on that topic and it be deducted from the Petkovic Defence time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vegar, let's go back to the first topic which I mentioned, which is Arif Pasalic's speech, and it is a document which, in preparing for the cross-examination yesterday, I didn't include in this set of documents, so you can find it in the Bruno Stojic Defence documents, and it is document 2D 00448. My colleague tells me that the document is in the second binder, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would the usher help the witness and show him Arif Pasalic's speech, because I'd like to focus on what I consider some important details. The document is in the second Stojic binder of the.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I am looking at the clock. Overall, the Defence has 38 minutes left. I don't know if Mr. Coric's Defence counsel wishes to say something.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before my colleague Dijana states her views, I would like to draw to your attention that the Praljak Defence said that he'd had received Defence time from Mr. Prlic, so that along with our 18 minutes, we have another 18 minutes at our disposal, which makes a total of 36 minutes. Now, if General Praljak used up more time, I don't think that that could be at the expense of the Petkovic Defence in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak spoke for 52 minutes. You have an hour and a half minus 58 minutes. You have 38 minutes left. We shall not be flexible on this matter. Thirty-eight minutes, and that is if Coric's Defence counsel doesn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I knew for certain that everybody conducting a cross-examination, whether it be the Defence or the Prosecution, that they would strictly adhere to what was discussed in the examination-in-chief and wouldn't be allowed by the Court to go beyond that, then in that case, after the examination-in-chief, I could state my views straight away and say whether I have questions or not. However, faced with a situation like that, in order to protect my client's interests, I can't say that at this stage. I don't think I'll have any questions, but I must keep at least a few minutes back for myself, if the need arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the questioning of Defence of General Praljak, you noted -- you said that some minutes will be taken out of account for the cross and will be deducted from our future account, so perhaps this should not be used in order to harm Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but we can't rule straight away. The Judges have differing views, and we cannot rule on this, whether time should be taken off Mr. Praljak's time. We shall see that later on. There's one hour and thirty minutes for the cross-examination. The witness is not a hostile witness vis-a-vis the other accused, and I have given my opinion on this. The cross-examination is, in fact, examination-in-chief. I wanted this to be recorded on the transcript. Ms. Alaburic, you have the floor, and we will finish at a quarter to 2:00.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Since this trial is going to go on for more than four years, I don't think it will be a great problem, whether I'm going to have 38 or 45 minutes at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vegar, you have found this speech by Arif Pasalic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly when you told us today that you and your colleagues did not like using the concept of war or term "war" for relations between Muslims and Croats in Mostar, even at the end of June, when the first serious clashes began? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let's see what Mr. Arif Pasalic says. Towards the end of the first page of the Croatian text, which is, for Their Honours' benefit, on page 2, line 5 and 6 of the English, Arif Pasalic says: "Rest assured that you declared war on us. This morning, you declared war." And then the last sentence of that whole speech: "You should know that hundreds and thousands of Hujkos will be born today, precisely against those of you who imposed war upon us." So, Mr. Vegar, I can conclude from that that Mr. Arif Pasalic considers that on the 30th of June, 1993, a war began between the Muslims and Croats in Mostar. Would you, as an analyst of this speech, agree with an observation of that kind?

utterances.speaker: VESO VEGAR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, the war in Mostar began earlier on. And the second point is we did not impose the war, so the people he is addressing -- Mr. Pasalic is addressing, well, especially not on that day, the 30th of June, when the units that he commanded launched an attack both in town and in the barracks and North Camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vegar, let me just tell you, I'm not asking you what you think happened then, but whether you, having read this speech by Mr. Pasalic, would interpret it as him saying that then on the 30th of June, war was declared, and that that's when the war began, because the sentence before that -- or, rather, the paragraph -- in the paragraph before that, he says that he was sitting in a cafe with a military commander, Vr lic, and with Puljic he created a joint command, and then he says, "You declared war upon us." Now, is it Arif Pasalic who considers that the war began on the 30th of June, 1993, based on this speech of his and what he says in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but one of the problems that recurs, Your Honours, is that if I wait for the translation, then often then we get the answer, and then it makes the objection a bit late in that sense, so it's difficult not to intervene earlier, before the witness has a chance to answer the question. Your Honour, I don't see how we're assisted by this. The Judges -- Your Honours can read the letter. Why -- what's the special added value having this particular witness read the letter and tell us what he thinks it means? Your Honours have it. You can read it. You can decide for yourself. But I don't see what this witness -- how this witness can add to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, it is better you put the question to the witness in this manner: "We have a document," and you sum up the contents of the document, and then you put your question. Otherwise, you can spend your entire time reading out the document wait for him to say "yes" or "no." What we are interested in is that you highlight your strategy, your defence. Otherwise, we are wasting our time. We are entitled, according to the Rules, to control the witness's testimony, and I would like you to put clear questions to the witness without reading out the entirety of the documents, and then you can put your question to the witness. Just sum it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I read out just ten words -- approximately ten words from the document, so I wasn't actually reading the document, the entirety of the document. And this question was asked of the witness because he dealt with relationships with the public and liaising with the public, and he was an expert in this area, and he could have analysed Arif Pasalic's speech and drawn conclusions about the effectiveness of that speech that was broadcast over the radio at 11.00 on the 30th of June.
